@graph.name: County Leader's Guide to Data
@graph.abstract: Stop treating data as an IT project. Use it as a public asset, make evidence safe to surface, and start changing decisions one meeting at a time.
@graph.description: A practical, executive-facing learning set adapted from the provided 'County Leader's Guide to Data'. The six source chapters are preserved as reusable narrative units; the leadership exercises, slides, and knowledge check were developed for this demo.

isBasedOn.name: County Leader's Guide to Data
isBasedOn.description: User-provided Markdown source used to create the original six narrative units.

@graph.name: Learning objectives
@graph.description: What a County leader should be able to explain or do after working through this guide.

@graph.name: Use data to make accountable County decisions
Distinguish file-bound information from structured, useful data
Balance public value with privacy, security, and integrity
Explain how transactional systems, dashboards, and data hygiene relate
Lead a practical change in County data culture
Ask for evidence and respond constructively to uncomfortable results
Distinguish the responsibilities of engineers, analysts, and stewards
Choose a small data-based change to an upcoming leadership decision
From Files to Facts
@graph.abstract: Most County information still sits in files. Structured, trackable facts can be sorted, combined, and used to anticipate service and budget needs.

@graph.name: Data Is a Public Trust
@graph.abstract: Treat County data as a public asset: use it to improve services and protect the people represented in it.

@graph.name: How County Data Works
@graph.abstract: Structured entries power operational records and leadership dashboards. Good data hygiene is essential to both.

@graph.name: Make Evidence Safe to Share
@graph.abstract: Reward transparency, ask for evidence, and do not turn a weak performance metric into a reason to hide information.

@graph.name: Builders, Interpreters, and Stewards
@graph.abstract: Engineers build the pipes, analysts turn facts into answers, and existing staff uphold data quality at its source.

@graph.name: Start Even Smaller
@graph.abstract: For the next major decision, require one usable operational fact. Ask for an evidence-based narrative before approving expansion.

@graph.name: Bring Better Evidence to the Next Meeting
@graph.abstract: Ask for a decision, measurable need, data limitations, alternatives, and a follow-up measure before approving a major request.

@graph.name: A First-Month Leadership Challenge
@graph.abstract: Make evidence routine: bring one fact, discuss its limits safely, name data owners and analysts, then revisit a decision.

County Leader's Guide to Data — Reading Material
@graph.abstract: Six direct leadership lessons, followed by two practical exercises for the next County decision.

@graph.text: Staff must manually extract and combine facts before they can be analyzed.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. A collection of files stores records but makes the underlying facts hard to sort and compare.

@graph.text: Scanned forms automatically provide standardized, queryable fields.
@graph.marin:feedback: Scanned images do not automatically create structured fields for filtering and comparison.

@graph.text: Charts are impossible unless the department buys a new server.
@graph.marin:feedback: The barrier described here is the structure of the information, not an inevitable server purchase.

@graph.text: The records have no value because they are not structured.
@graph.marin:feedback: Existing files can hold valuable information, but extracting it is labor-intensive.

@graph.name: A department has years of scanned service forms. Leadership wants to compare demand over time. What is the most important limitation of relying on the forms alone?
@graph.text: A department has years of scanned service forms. Leadership wants to compare demand over time. What is the most important limitation of relying on the forms alone?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about what someone would have to do before counting the same field across hundreds of forms.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide contrasts file-bound documents with individual trackable facts that can be filtered, sorted, and combined.

@graph.text: The time a particular 911 dispatch was recorded.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. A timestamp is one individual trackable fact.

@graph.text: A directory of PDF incident reports.
@graph.marin:feedback: A folder of reports is a document collection, even though it contains facts.

@graph.text: A scanned packet of permit applications.
@graph.marin:feedback: A scanned packet is unstructured source material, not one discrete field value.

@graph.text: A binder of quarterly department summaries.
@graph.marin:feedback: A binder collects reports; it is not itself one individually trackable unit of fact.

@graph.name: Which example is a single data point rather than a collection of files?
@graph.text: Which example is a single data point rather than a collection of files?
@graph.marin:hint: Distinguish an individual value from the container holding many values.
@graph.marin:explanation: The original guide offers individual locations, timestamps, and parcel values as examples of data points.

@graph.text: Use reliable information to improve services and resource allocation.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Stewardship involves extracting value for public services.

@graph.text: Protect the privacy and integrity of sensitive information.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. A steward has an explicit duty to protect affected people and the records about them.

@graph.text: Circulate all individual records across departments whenever someone asks.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. The guide calls for secure sharing, not unrestricted circulation.

@graph.text: Treat the department as the permanent owner that can veto every appropriate use.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. The guide challenges territorial claims and emphasizes collective public stewardship.

@graph.name: A County data steward is balancing public value and public trust. Which responsibilities belong in that balance? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: A County data steward is balancing public value and public trust. Which responsibilities belong in that balance? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: The guide makes stewardship a two-sided obligation, not a choice between value and protection.
@graph.marin:explanation: Good stewardship both delivers public benefit and protects sensitive information; neither blanket secrecy nor blanket disclosure meets the standard.

@graph.text: Clarify the purpose and use an appropriately authorized, privacy-protective way to share the needed facts.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Secure collaboration should preserve the purpose of the analysis and the people represented in the data.

@graph.text: Release every record because departments are co-stewards.
@graph.marin:feedback: Co-stewardship does not eliminate the need to protect sensitive information.

@graph.text: Refuse any collaboration because the source department owns the records.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide rejects territorial ownership as the basis for blocking appropriate collaboration.

@graph.text: Send unreviewed files and ask the receiving team to handle the risk.
@graph.marin:feedback: Passing along sensitive records without safeguards neglects stewardship obligations.

@graph.name: A program asks another department for person-level records to understand a service trend. Which leadership response best reflects the guide?
@graph.text: A program asks another department for person-level records to understand a service trend. Which leadership response best reflects the guide?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about both sides of stewardship: useful cooperation and safeguarding sensitive details.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide urges secure cross-department sharing while defending the privacy, security, and integrity of sensitive data.

@graph.text: Record operational facts when staff perform day-to-day work.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Dispatch and permitting tools are examples of transactional systems.

@graph.text: Evaluate the County's long-range financial strategy for executives.
@graph.marin:feedback: Strategic interpretation belongs more closely to analysis and leadership decisions.

@graph.text: Replace the need for data hygiene and consistent definitions.
@graph.marin:feedback: Transactions still need accurate and standardized entries.

@graph.text: Publish only completed dashboard graphics for the public.
@graph.marin:feedback: Dashboards are analytical outputs, not the core transactional input process.

@graph.name: In the guide, what does a transactional system primarily do?
@graph.text: In the guide, what does a transactional system primarily do?
@graph.marin:hint: Consider where an operational fact enters a system for the first time.
@graph.marin:explanation: Transactional tools are used by frontline staff to enter or update operational facts.

@graph.text: An analytical dashboard drawing on operational data.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Dashboards transform operational records into charts, maps, and patterns for leadership.

@graph.text: A scanned filing cabinet that stores each request as a PDF.
@graph.marin:feedback: A digital filing cabinet preserves documents but does not by itself produce trend analysis.

@graph.text: A separate spreadsheet with different definitions for each program.
@graph.marin:feedback: Inconsistent definitions make comparison unreliable.

@graph.text: A permitting portal limited to entering individual applications.
@graph.marin:feedback: A permitting portal is primarily transactional rather than an executive analysis layer.

@graph.name: A County executive wants a cross-program chart of demand trends. Which kind of system is intended to make the big picture visible?
@graph.text: A County executive wants a cross-program chart of demand trends. Which kind of system is intended to make the big picture visible?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about the difference between capturing an event and interpreting many events together.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide distinguishes transactional input systems from analytical systems used to see patterns and trends.

@graph.text: Agree on consistent field definitions and permitted values.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Shared definitions prevent similar facts from being counted differently.

@graph.text: Identify incomplete or duplicated sensitive records before they drive decisions.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Completeness, accuracy, and careful handling are central to data hygiene.

@graph.text: Let each team invent a different abbreviation for the same street name.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. This reproduces the inconsistent naming problem raised in the guide.

@graph.text: Stop checking entries once a dashboard looks convincing.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. A convincing chart cannot compensate for unreliable underlying data.

@graph.name: Which changes would improve data hygiene across County programs? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: Which changes would improve data hygiene across County programs? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Look for actions that make the same fact mean the same thing in different systems.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide's street-name example illustrates standardization; it also links poor quality to flawed policy and sensitive-record handling.

@graph.text: Thank the team for surfacing the issue, examine the facts, and decide what to improve.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. A culture that rewards transparency makes reliable reporting more likely.

@graph.text: Remove the metric from the next report so the department avoids criticism.
@graph.marin:feedback: Hiding weak performance eliminates the information needed to improve.

@graph.text: Assume staff are incompetent based on one chart.
@graph.marin:feedback: Punitive conclusions from a metric discourage candid reporting.

@graph.text: Require the team to improve the reported value before discussing its cause.
@graph.marin:feedback: Changing the number without improving the process damages trust in the data.

@graph.name: A dashboard shows that a service target was missed. What leadership response is most likely to keep accurate reporting alive?
@graph.text: A dashboard shows that a service target was missed. What leadership response is most likely to keep accurate reporting alive?
@graph.marin:hint: Consider what a team will report next month if sharing uncomfortable evidence triggers punishment.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide argues that weaponized metrics produce avoidance and manipulation; leaders should protect transparency and investigate.

@graph.text: What data supports that conclusion?
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. The guide specifically asks leaders to require evidence for staffing claims.

@graph.text: Which other department can we copy without checking its workload?
@graph.marin:feedback: Copying staffing levels without relevant evidence skips the analysis.

@graph.text: Can we remove the request from the agenda until next fiscal year?
@graph.marin:feedback: Deferral does not test the underlying claim.

@graph.text: Which chart will look most persuasive regardless of its source?
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide advocates evidence, not decorative justification.

@graph.name: A manager says a division is severely understaffed. What is the first leadership question recommended by the guide?
@graph.text: A manager says a division is severely understaffed. What is the first leadership question recommended by the guide?
@graph.marin:hint: The guide proposes a short question that changes the meeting's currency.
@graph.marin:explanation: The leadership habit is to ask to see the underlying evidence rather than decide from volume of complaints or intuition.

@graph.text: Data engineers create secure pathways among isolated systems.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Building infrastructure and moving data are engineering responsibilities.

@graph.text: Data analysts turn operational numbers into meaningful answers for leaders.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Analysts interpret information in the context of County services.

@graph.text: Existing managers and frontline staff help enforce reliable data entry.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Day-to-day stewardship is part of existing operating responsibilities.

@graph.text: Executive dashboards automatically fix inconsistent data entries.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. A dashboard cannot replace data-entry quality and stewardship.

@graph.name: Which role-to-responsibility matches follow the guide? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: Which role-to-responsibility matches follow the guide? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Separate who builds data pathways, who interprets results, and who protects data quality at entry.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide distinguishes builders (engineers), interpreters (analysts), and enforcers (stewards already embedded in operations).

@graph.text: Use specialized build capacity initially, retain ongoing analytical context internally, and make data quality a responsibility of current operations staff.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. The guide differentiates temporary specialized engineering, ongoing internal interpretation, and routine stewardship.

@graph.text: Hire a permanent team of external analysts with no operational context and leave data-entry quality unassigned.
@graph.marin:feedback: Analytical work benefits from operational knowledge, and data quality needs accountable staff.

@graph.text: Treat infrastructure maintenance and analytical interpretation as interchangeable roles.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide explicitly separates building pipelines from making sense of their outputs.

@graph.text: Let each department build undocumented pipelines without long-term support planning.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide emphasizes standards, documentation, and maintainable architecture.

@graph.name: For a new cross-department data architecture, which staffing model most closely matches the guide?
@graph.text: For a new cross-department data architecture, which staffing model most closely matches the guide?
@graph.marin:hint: Match the likely duration of the work to the role's need for ongoing County context.
@graph.marin:explanation: The source recommends careful sourcing of specialist build work while emphasizing institutional knowledge for analysts and existing staff ownership of hygiene.

@graph.text: Require one well-defined operational measure for the next major agenda decision.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. A meeting expectation is a small change with direct leadership influence.

@graph.text: Wait until every department has a replacement software platform.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide rejects an all-at-once overhaul as a prerequisite.

@graph.text: Build an enterprise dashboard before asking which decision it should inform.
@graph.marin:feedback: Starting with technology rather than the decision reverses the guide's emphasis.

@graph.text: Stop data reviews until all historical records are error-free.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide recommends beginning with imperfect information and improving it.

@graph.name: Which action best reflects the guide's instruction to start "even smaller"?
@graph.text: Which action best reflects the guide's instruction to start "even smaller"?
@graph.marin:hint: Look for an action a department head can take at the very next meeting.
@graph.marin:explanation: The immediate change is to require structured evidence for important decisions, not to start with a multi-million-dollar platform replacement.

@graph.text: A clear statement of the decision and the service need.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Decision-makers need to know what action the facts are meant to support.

@graph.text: Measures with definitions, time periods, and known limitations.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. Without context and limitations, a number can mislead.

@graph.text: A follow-up measure showing whether the change worked.
@graph.marin:feedback: Yes. A decision should be reviewed against an observable result.

@graph.text: A persuasive anecdote presented as a substitute for operational records.
@graph.marin:feedback: No. An anecdote may identify a question but should not replace the requested structured evidence.

@graph.name: Before approving a substantial program expansion, which elements make an evidence-based request more useful? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: Before approving a substantial program expansion, which elements make an evidence-based request more useful? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Think about the before, during, and after of a major decision.
@graph.marin:explanation: The practical exercise asks for a defined decision, meaningful measures, quality limitations, alternatives, and a way to evaluate the result.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: Choosing True treats a technology overhaul as a prerequisite, which the guide explicitly rejects.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: Choosing False follows the guide: change meeting habits and ask for better evidence before pursuing a sweeping overhaul.

@graph.name: A County must complete a multi-million-dollar technology overhaul before leaders can begin making data-driven decisions.
@graph.text: A County must complete a multi-million-dollar technology overhaul before leaders can begin making data-driven decisions.
@graph.marin:hint: Consider the size of the first step the author recommends.
@graph.marin:explanation: The source advocates small executive habits rather than an immediate comprehensive technology project.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: Choosing True recognizes the guide's closing advice: reveal the imperfections and begin cleaning them up.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: Choosing False assumes imperfect data must be hidden until fixed, contrary to the guide's advice to embrace the mess.

@graph.name: An imperfect first data extract can still be useful if leaders acknowledge its limitations and begin improving the quality.
@graph.text: An imperfect first data extract can still be useful if leaders acknowledge its limitations and begin improving the quality.
@graph.marin:hint: Think about how leaders should react when their first report contains errors.
@graph.marin:explanation: The guide closes by treating messy data as the beginning of improvement, not proof that the effort has failed.

@graph.text: Clarify data definitions, assign responsibility for quality, and revisit a decision using the same measure.
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Repeatable measures and clear operating responsibilities turn a one-time request into a management habit.

@graph.text: Ask for a different, undocumented metric at every meeting.
@graph.marin:feedback: Changing definitions unpredictably undermines comparison and accountability.

@graph.text: Delegate all decisions to a dashboard without discussion of context.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide sees dashboards as tools for informed leadership, not automatic decision-makers.

@graph.text: Stop asking questions when the first report contains mistakes.
@graph.marin:feedback: The guide argues that the first messy report is the moment to begin improving data quality.

@graph.name: A director has started requesting operational evidence. What next step best makes that habit sustainable?
@graph.text: A director has started requesting operational evidence. What next step best makes that habit sustainable?
@graph.marin:hint: Consider which steps make data work repeatable rather than performative.
@graph.marin:explanation: The added first-month exercise emphasizes consistent measures, responsibility for data quality, constructive review, and follow-through.

@graph.name: Data leadership knowledge check

marin:gradeBands.name: A
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Excellent. You are ready to ask for evidence, protect the public trust, and make it safe to tell the truth.

marin:gradeBands.name: B
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Strong work. Keep turning good questions into routine leadership habits.

marin:gradeBands.name: C
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: A sound start. Review the explanations and sharpen the link between data quality and decisions.

marin:gradeBands.name: D
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: The next meeting is an opportunity to improve. Revisit the stewardship and data-hygiene sections.

marin:gradeBands.name: F
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Start smaller. Read the guide again, then ask what evidence you would need before making a decision.

@graph.name: Data Leadership Knowledge Check
@graph.abstract: Ten randomized questions test evidence-based leadership, public stewardship, data hygiene, and realistic next steps.

@graph.name: County Leader's Guide to Data
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Open by asking: When was the last time a County decision changed because a leader asked to see the underlying facts?

@graph.name: Data Is a Leadership Issue
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Keep this about public administration, not software procurement. Files and data are different ways of making information usable.

@graph.name: Files Preserve Records. Data Reveals Patterns.
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Contrast static documents with individual measurable facts. Use a pothole location or dispatch timestamp as an example.

@graph.name: Use the Asset. Protect the People.
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: The guide frames data stewardship as a two-sided public obligation. Secure collaboration and privacy safeguards are not competing priorities.

@graph.name: From Entry to Insight
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Transactional systems capture events; analytical views help interpret many events. Do not imply a dashboard improves bad inputs on its own.

@graph.name: Garbage In, Garbage Out
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Ask participants whether two programs use the same definitions for the measures on their dashboards.

@graph.name: Reward the Uncomfortable Truth
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: When a metric is missed, the initial response determines whether staff will report the next problem. Transparency is a precondition for improvement.

@graph.name: Show Me the Data
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Use the guide's central management question: “Show me the data that leads you to that conclusion.” Ask for interpretation, not only a chart.

@graph.name: Builders, Interpreters, Stewards
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Separate specialist engineering work from ongoing interpretation and daily data quality. The source suggests contractors or specialists for an initial build, internal analysts, and existing staff as stewards.

@graph.name: Start Even Smaller
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: The guide recommends changing a meeting agenda and the evidence expected with major requests before seeking an expansive platform build.

@graph.name: Put the Next Decision to the Test
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Invite learners to name one pending decision and the facts needed to defend it. Discuss definitions, privacy, and alternative courses.

@graph.name: Make It a Habit
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: This is an illustrative practice plan added for the learning package, not a County-adopted policy or schedule.

@graph.name: Embrace the Mess. Then Improve It.
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Close by reminding leaders that incomplete first data extracts are not proof of failure. Start cleaning one fact at a time.

@graph.name: County Leader's Guide to Data — Slide Deck
@graph.abstract: A concise presentation for leadership discussions about data, trust, capability, and habits.
